Hi Alex / Samira — thanks for the clear list. Below are short, actionable answers plus example snippets. Happy to expand any of these in the workshop.

1) Auth / token exchange:
- Redwood supports both patterns: server-proxying with long-lived API keys and delegated short-lived tokens via our STS-style exchange. For hosted customers we recommend issuing short-lived tokens scoped to a route (min TTL 5m) and rotating them via your auth backend. We integrate with common KMS/HSMs for key wrapping.
- If you need end-user identity propagation (e.g., per-customer auditing), use short-lived tokens exchanged via your backend. Proxying works too but adds latency and operational overhead.

Example (pseudo):
- Step A: Your backend calls Redwood Token Exchange API with service credentials -> Redwood returns short-lived client_token (scoped: model:xyz, route:search).
- Step B: Client uses client_token in Authorization: Bearer <client_token> for streaming calls.

Attachments: sdk_auth_flow.png (attached)

2) Chat vs completions (practical diffs):
- Chat endpoint is optimized for multi-turn context, system/instruction roles, and tool calling; it maintains message metadata (role, name) which makes tool invocation easier. It also has better built-in structured output tooling (tool calls and JSON schema enforcement).
- Completions endpoint is simpler (single prompt -> text) and can be slightly cheaper for one-off completions. However, for structured tool calling and fine-grained streaming semantics, chat is recommended.

Behavioral diffs relevant to you:
- stop sequences: both endpoints support stop tokens; chat adds an additional layer: instruction/system messages can implicitly constrain output. If you need strict JSON, use the JSON schema option on chat + stop tokens as a fallback.
- streaming: both endpoints stream token deltas. Chat streaming includes role markers and tool call boundaries so the client can detect when the model is trying to invoke a tool vs emitting text.

3) Tokenization & max_tokens:
- Redwood exposes an SDK helper to estimate token usage client-side using the same tokenizer as the serving runtime. We recommend using that to get pre-call token estimates.
- For large prompts (~8k tokens in customer data) consider: prefix caching (cache common system + retrieval context), truncation policies (prioritize most relevant retrieved chunks), and using embeddings to pre-rank so less context is necessary.
- max_tokens: set to the expected response length + buffer. On chat, max_tokens applies to the generated portion (not counting input tokens) — enforced by the server.

4) Streaming and structured JSON / tool-calls:
- Streaming will emit partial tokens which can break JSON if you try to parse mid-stream. Recommended patterns:
  - Client renders progressive plain-text UI from stream deltas.
  - For structured outputs, use the chat JSON schema enforcement: Redwood validates the final output against the schema server-side and can either error or provide a best-effort corrected JSON. You can also request the model to emit a final JSON block at the end (use a unique delimiter + stop sequence).
  - Tool-calls: chat streaming includes explicit tool call start/end markers in the stream so your client can buffer the tool payload until complete, then invoke the tool.

Example payloads (short):
- Chat (tool call + JSON schema):
POST /v1/chat/completions
Authorization: Bearer <token>
{
  "model": "redwood-chat-1",
  "messages": [
    {"role":"system", "content":"You are a structured assistant."},
    {"role":"user", "content":"Search for 'sprocket maintenance' and return a JSON list of top 3 docs with id, score, snippet."}
  ],
  "json_schema": {"type":"object","properties":{"results":{"type":"array"}}},
  "stream": true
}

- Completions (one-off):
POST /v1/completions
Authorization: Bearer <token>
{
  "model": "redwood-complete-1",
  "prompt": "Extract top 3 documents for query: sprocket maintenance:\n1) ",
  "max_tokens": 256,
  "stop": ["\n\n"]
}

Practical recommendation: standardize on chat for multi-turn + tool-calls + structured responses; use completions for simple one-shot transforms.
